bullets: How slicing, signing and substituting turn area under a curve into exact answers: Riemann sums, u-substitution and volumes of revolution
slides.heading: JC H2 integration: Riemann sums, u-substitution, volumes of revolution
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build integration from the ground up - area sliced into rectangles, area that can go negative, a substitution that runs the chain rule backwards, and discs stacked into a volume - and by the end you will know exactly when the +C belongs and when it does not.

bullets: Evaluate definite integrals as limits of Riemann sums and as signed area, such as the integral of x from -1 to 2 giving 3/2
Use u-substitution and the disc method: the integral of 2x e^(x^2) from 0 to 1 is e - 1, and rotating y = x^2 from 0 to 1 gives volume pi/5
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap about adding +C to a definite integral.

bullets: Four rectangles under y = x^2 from 0 to 2 estimate the area as 3.75, but the true area is 8/3, about 2.67
Eight narrower rectangles tighten the estimate to 3.1875 - so what happens with a hundred, or a thousand?
slides.heading: How much area hides under a curve?
slides.notes: Ask the class to commit to a guess before any formulas: the rectangles overshoot every time here, so does the estimate shrink toward the truth as the strips narrow? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the limit of those sums is the integral itself.

bullets: A definite integral is the limit of Riemann sums: slice the interval, multiply each width by a height, add, then let the slices thin to nothing
Area below the x-axis counts as negative, so a definite integral gives net signed area, not total area
The fundamental theorem links the two worlds: if F differentiates to f, the integral of f from a to b is F(b) - F(a)
slides.heading: One symbol, three faces: sums, areas, antiderivatives
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: the integral is not a trick for antiderivatives - it is a limit of sums first, and the antiderivative shortcut works precisely because of that limit.

bullets: Four wide rectangles under y = x^2 from 0 to 2 give 3.75; eight narrow ones give 3.1875, closing in on the exact 8/3
Thinner slices leave less overhang: the Riemann sum becomes the integral exactly in the limit as the width goes to zero
slides.heading: Riemann sums: slicing area under a curve
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the strips halve in width and hug the curve tighter - nothing is being guessed, the sum is converging on the one true area, 8/3.

bullets: The triangle of y = x above the axis from 0 to 2 contributes +2; the triangle below the axis from -1 to 0 contributes -0.5
Net signed area: 2 - 0.5 = 1.5, so the integral of x from -1 to 2 is exactly 3/2
slides.heading: Signed area: below the axis counts negative
slides.notes: Stress the sign rule with the colours: green above the axis adds, red below the axis subtracts. If a question asks for total area instead, split at the crossing and add the magnitudes - but the integral itself always reports the signed net.

bullets: The integral of 2x e^(x^2) from 0 to 1 hides a chain rule: the 2x is exactly the derivative of the inner x^2
Set u = x^2, so du = 2x dx and the limits 0 and 1 stay 0 and 1 in u: the integral becomes the integral of e^u, giving e - 1
slides.heading: u-substitution: the chain rule in reverse
slides.notes: Work the substitution in two beats: first spot the inner function and check its derivative is sitting outside, then rewrite everything - integrand, differential and limits - in u before integrating. Never mix x-limits with a u-integrand.

bullets: Rotating y = x^2 about the x-axis from 0 to 1 sweeps a trumpet shape; slicing across the axis gives discs of radius x^2 and thickness dx
Each disc has volume pi r^2 dx = pi (x^2)^2 dx, and stacking them gives V = pi times the integral of x^4 from 0 to 1, which is pi/5
slides.heading: Volumes of revolution: stacking discs
slides.notes: Point at the discs growing along the axis and say: the method is Riemann sums again, one dimension up - slice, approximate each slice as a plain cylinder, add, and let the thickness go to zero.

bullets: The trap claim is: A definite integral still needs the +C in the answer.
An indefinite integral names a whole family of antiderivatives, so it needs +C; a definite integral evaluates one antiderivative at two limits, and the +C cancels in the subtraction
slides.heading: The +C trap: only for indefinite integrals
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: write the +C inside the bracket if it helps you see it - (8/3 + C) - (1/3 + C) - and watch it vanish, leaving exactly 7/3.

bullets: Step 1: antiderivative first: the integral of x^2 is x^3/3, so the definite integral is [x^3/3] from 1 to 2
Step 2: evaluate at the limits: 8/3 - 1/3 = 7/3 - a single number, with no +C anywhere in the final answer
slides.heading: Worked example: the integral of x^2 from 1 to 2
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: the bracket notation is the promise that two evaluations and one subtraction are coming, and a subtraction is exactly where any constant would cancel.

bullets: Find the integral of 2x e^(x^2) from 0 to 1 using u = x^2, changing the differential and checking the limits as you go
Careful - a classmate finishes a definite integral and writes: A definite integral still needs the +C in the answer. Explain to them why the constant cancels at the two limits
slides.heading: Your turn: integrate, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the substitution bookkeeping first, then on the exact sentence they used to talk their classmate out of the +C.

bullets: On your own: evaluate the integral of x^2 from 1 to 2 and state the volume when y = x^2 is rotated about the x-axis from 0 to 1
Watch out for the trap one last time: A definite integral still needs the +C in the answer. Say when +C is genuinely needed
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for clean limit evaluation in your first answer and one clear sentence separating definite from indefinite integrals in your second.
